summary: Specifies how IS-IS carries IPv6 traffic engineering information so routers can compute traffic-engineered routes that use IPv6 addresses. It is a proposed standard.

eli5.summary: Routers share maps showing which roads have room. This lets them share those maps for the newer style of internet addresses too.

questions: what is ipv6 traffic engineering in is-is
what is the ipv6 srlg tlv
what is tlv type 140 in is-is
what is the ipv6 global interface address tlv
subtitle: New IS-IS TLVs that let routers advertise traffic engineering information using IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The IS-IS traffic engineering TLVs identify routers and links with IPv4 addresses, so they cannot describe traffic-engineered links in IPv6 networks.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines IPv6 equivalents: an IPv6 TE Router ID TLV (type 140), IPv6 Interface Address and Neighbor Address sub-TLVs (types 12 and 13), an IPv6 SRLG TLV (type 139) and an IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV (type 233).
tldr.outcome: Routers in an IS-IS network can carry traffic engineering information, including GMPLS information, for IPv6 and calculate traffic-engineered routes with IPv6 addresses. The RFC is a Proposed Standard.

today: RFC 6119 is a Proposed Standard published in February 2011, and no later RFC obsoletes or updates it according to its metadata. It builds on RFC 5305, RFC 5307 and RFC 5308.

sections.title: Why IS-IS Needs IPv6 TE TLVs
sections.content:
In IS-IS, each router generates a Link State PDU (LSP) describing itself and its links. The information is encoded as TLVs (Type, Length, Value). RFC 5305 and RFC 5307 define TLVs and sub-TLVs that carry traffic engineering (TE) and GMPLS information, but the addressing in them is IPv4 specific.

RFC 5308 shows how IS-IS can run Shortest Path First routing for IPv6 with IPv6-specific TLVs. This document does the same job for traffic engineering. As the RFC puts it, MPLS traffic engineering is very successful, and as IPv6 use grows there is a need to support it in IPv6 networks.
sections.eli5: The old maps could only name roads using the old address style. This document adds a way to name them with the new address style.

sections.title: Identifying Links with IPv6 Addresses
sections.content:
A link has properties such as bandwidth, shared risk link groups (SRLGs) and switching capabilities. When IPv6 is used, a numbered link may be identified by IPv4 and/or IPv6 interface addresses. The kind of identifier does not change the link's properties.

An IPv6 address can have global, unique-local or link-local scope. Because the IPv6 TE TLVs are propagated across networks, they MUST NOT use link-local addresses. IS-IS does not need to tell global and unique-local addresses apart.

Each IPv4 address used in the existing TE TLVs gets an IPv6 counterpart: the TE Router ID TLV, the Interface Address and Neighbor Address sub-TLVs, and the SRLG TLV.
sections.eli5: Every road gets a name that works everywhere in the city, not a nickname that only makes sense on one street.

sections.title: The Router ID and Address TLVs
sections.content:
The IPv6 TE Router ID TLV is type 140 and holds a 16-octet IPv6 address. It must be a stable global address, so the router ID stays routable whatever state the node's interfaces are in. A router that implements IPv6 TE MUST include it in its LSP, and it MUST NOT appear more than once in an LSP.

Two sub-TLVs of the Extended IS Reachability TLV carry link addresses. The IPv6 Interface Address sub-TLV is type 12 and the IPv6 Neighbor Address sub-TLV is type 13. Both hold a 16-octet address, can occur multiple times, and MUST NOT hold a link-local address. A router that implements IPv6 TE MUST include them, except on an unnumbered point-to-point link, where the Link-Local Interface Identifiers sub-TLV is used instead. The Neighbor Address sub-TLV is required for point-to-point links.

Receivers MUST NOT treat the router ID, or the interface addresses, as a /128 reachable prefix in routing or forwarding. Doing so can cause forwarding loops when interacting with systems that do not support these TLVs.

To learn the neighbor's global address, the RFC adds the IPv6 Global Interface Address TLV, type 233. It goes in IIH (Hello) PDUs, never in LSPs, and carries the global or unique-local addresses of the interface sending the Hello. This is needed because the IPv6 Interface Address TLV from RFC 5308 only holds link-local addresses in a Hello.
sections.eli5: Each router gets a permanent name tag, and each road gets a label on both ends. Routers also say hello with their city-wide address so neighbors can write it down.

sections.title: The IPv6 SRLG TLV
sections.content:
Links that would fail together, such as fibers in the same duct, share a risk. The IPv6 SRLG TLV (type 139) carries Shared Risk Link Group information. The older SRLG TLV (type 138) cannot be extended backward-compatibly to name a link by IPv6 addresses, so a new TLV was needed.

Its value holds a 6-octet System ID, 1 octet of pseudonode number, 1 octet of flags, a 16-octet IPv6 interface address, an optional 16-octet IPv6 neighbor address, and a list of 4-octet SRLG values. The length is 24 + 4 * (number of SRLG values), plus 16 if the neighbor address is included.

The flags octet has one defined bit, NA, which says whether the neighbor address is present. Unknown bits MUST be sent as zero. A receiver that sees a non-zero bit it does not understand MUST ignore the TLV, but still floods it unchanged. This leaves room for future ways of identifying a link.

To avoid confusion with type 138: the IPv6 SRLG TLV may occur more than once in an LSP, but there MUST NOT be more than one for a given link. It MUST NOT be used if the link can be described with the type 138 TLV, and if a receiver gets both for the same link it MUST apply the type 138 TLV and ignore the IPv6 one.
sections.eli5: Some roads run through the same tunnel, so one landslide would block them all. This tells everyone which roads share a tunnel, using the new address style.

sections.title: Security and Migration
sections.content:
The RFC says it raises no new security issues for IS-IS. For general IS-IS security it points to RFC 5304, which covers IS-IS cryptographic authentication.

On migration, the extensions allow routing of GMPLS Label Switched Paths using IPv6 addressing through an IS-IS network. Adding this IPv6 TE routing information to an existing IPv4 GMPLS network causes no migration issues. Moving Label Switched Paths from IPv4 to IPv6 is a GMPLS signaling matter and out of scope.
sections.eli5: Nothing here makes the mail system less safe, and adding the new labels does not break the old ones.

sections.title: Registered Code Points
sections.content:
IANA registered three new IS-IS TLV types: 139 (IPv6 SRLG, used in LSPs), 140 (IPv6 TE Router ID, used in LSPs) and 233 (IPv6 Global Interface Address, used in IIH PDUs). None of them are used in SNPs.

IANA also registered two new sub-TLVs of TLV 22: type 12 (IPv6 Interface Address) and type 13 (IPv6 Neighbor Address), each with length 16. They are also valid under TLVs 141 and 222.
sections.eli5: Each new label got its own official number so every router reads it the same way.

viz.caption: VALUE FIELD OF THE IPV6 SRLG TLV (RFC 6119)

fields.name: Pseudonode num
fields.desc: Pseudonode number if the neighbor is on a LAN interface.

fields.name: Flags
fields.desc: NA bit set to 1 when the neighbor address is included.

fields.name: IPv6 neighbor address (optional)
fields.desc: 16 octets, present when NA is set.
